### Why CUDA Graph Replay is Faster

The primary reason a CUDA graph replay is faster than launching the same kernels eagerly is the **reduction of CPU-side overhead**. When you launch kernels eagerly, the CPU must perform a series of expensive operations for each kernel: it validates parameters, allocates resources, and makes a system call to the driver to enqueue the work on the GPU. This process, known as kernel launch overhead, involves significant CPU-to-GPU communication and synchronization. For workloads with many small, fast-running kernels, this CPU overhead can become the bottleneck, leaving the GPU idle while it waits for the next kernel to be launched.

A CUDA graph, by contrast, pre-defines the entire sequence of operations, their dependencies, and their parameters. This entire structure is captured once and stored on the GPU. When you "replay" the graph, the CPU's job is drastically simplified. Instead of launching dozens or hundreds of individual kernels, it issues a single, lightweight command to the GPU to execute the entire pre-defined graph.
